title: Design change data capture (CDC)
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, log-based capture, snapshots, ordering and delivery, schema evolution, outbox, operations. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Change data capture (CDC) turns every insert, update and delete in a database into an ordered stream of events that other systems can consume. Instead of asking the database "what changed?" with repeated queries, you read its own change log. Debezium, AWS DMS, Maxwell, Oracle GoldenGate, Postgres logical decoding and MySQL binlog readers do this. It is the backbone for keeping search indexes, caches, warehouses and microservices in sync.

Functional requirements

  • Capture all row changes (insert, update, delete) from source databases (MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB).
  • Publish them as events (before and after images, operation type, transaction id, timestamp) to a stream.
  • Support an initial snapshot of existing data, then continuous streaming without gaps or duplicates in meaning.
  • Deliver to many consumers: Elasticsearch, Redis, data warehouse, other services.
  • Handle schema changes (add column, rename).

Non-functional requirements

  • Low latency: typically under 1 s from commit to event.
  • Per-row ordering preserved; no change lost; consumers tolerate duplicates (at-least-once).
  • Minimal impact on the source database (a CDC reader must not slow the production primary).
  • Recoverable: restart from the last position without re-snapshotting.

Decision gravity. Choose log-based CDC (read the WAL/binlog) over query-based polling or dual writes. It is the only approach that sees deletes, preserves order, and adds almost no load to the source. Dual writes from the application are the classic trap and are very hard to undo once data has diverged.

Everyday analogy. Instead of repeatedly photographing a notice board to spot changes, you read the clerk's logbook of every change he made.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing "poll with updated_at > last_run": misses deletes and out-of-order commits.
  • Dual-writing to DB and Kafka from app code without a transaction.
  • Forgetting the initial snapshot.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
CDC is mostly infrastructure, but it has two APIs: a control plane (manage connectors) and the event contract consumers see.

Control plane (Kafka Connect REST, as used by Debezium):

POST /connectors
{ "name": "orders-pg",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "database.hostname": "pg-primary.internal", "database.port": "5432",
    "database.user": "cdc_reader", "database.dbname": "shop",
    "plugin.name": "pgoutput", "slot.name": "orders_slot", "publication.name": "orders_pub",
    "table.include.list": "public.orders,public.order_items",
    "topic.prefix": "shop", "snapshot.mode": "initial",
    "tasks.max": "1" } }
201 Created
GET    /connectors/orders-pg/status
POST   /connectors/orders-pg/restart
DELETE /connectors/orders-pg

Property names follow Debezium 2.x; confirm exact keys against the docs of your version.

Event contract (one Kafka message per row change; topic shop.public.orders, key = primary key):

{ "before": { "id": 9001, "status": "PAID" },
  "after":  { "id": 9001, "status": "SHIPPED" },
  "op": "u",                      // c create, u update, d delete, r snapshot read
  "ts_ms": 1731150000123,
  "source": { "db":"shop", "table":"orders", "lsn": 2849201123, "txId": 77123 } }

Consumers read with a consumer group and use source.lsn (or Kafka offset) for ordering and deduplication.

Industry example. LinkedIn built Databus for the same purpose, Netflix built DBLog (and uses it for snapshots without locking), and Debezium (Red Hat) is the common open-source choice. Airbnb's SpinalTap and Uber use similar log readers.

Everyday analogy. The control plane is hiring a court stenographer; the event contract is the format of the transcript pages.

Common interview traps.

  • Message key not set to the primary key (loses per-row ordering across partitions).
  • Treating the event schema as private; it is a public contract that other teams depend on.
  • Omitting the before image so consumers cannot compute deltas.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume an orders database with 5,000 writes/s peak, average row change event 1 KB (with before and after).

Quantity Calculation Result
Event rate 5,000 row changes/s 5,000 events/s
Throughput 5,000 x 1 KB 5 MB/s
Daily 5 MB/s x 86,400 ~430 GB/day (before compression; 3-4x smaller with LZ4/zstd)
Kafka retention 3 days, RF 3 430 GB x 3 x 3 / 3 (compressed) ~1.3 TB
Snapshot 500 GB table, read at 100 MB/s ~85 min
WAL growth if reader stalls 5 MB/s of WAL x 3600 ~18 GB per hour
Consumers 5 groups, each reads full stream 25 MB/s out of Kafka

What this tells you. Throughput is modest, one connector task is enough; Kafka is not the bottleneck. The dangerous number is the WAL growth when the CDC reader is down: the database keeps all logs the reader has not confirmed (a Postgres replication slot pins WAL), and a forgotten slot can fill the primary's disk and take down production.

Everyday analogy. A clerk who refuses to throw away logbook pages until the reader has copied them; if the reader vanishes, the pile blocks the office.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing only Kafka and forgetting source WAL retention.
  • Large multi-GB updates (bulk backfill) creating event storms.
  • Ignoring snapshot duration.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Log reader / connector: connects as a fake replica, reads Postgres WAL via logical replication (pgoutput/wal2json), MySQL binlog (ROW format, binlog_row_image=FULL), MongoDB oplog or change streams; converts to events.
  • Kafka (and Kafka Connect): durable, partitioned, replayable event bus; connector offsets stored in a Connect topic.
  • Schema registry (Avro/Protobuf): versioned schemas with compatibility rules (backward/forward) so consumers survive column changes.
  • Sinks: Kafka Connect sink connectors or custom consumers into Elasticsearch, S3/Iceberg, Redis, other DBs.
  • Monitoring: connector lag, replication slot lag, WAL size, DLQ rate.

Source configuration (Postgres)

# postgresql.conf
wal_level = logical
max_replication_slots = 10
max_wal_senders = 10
max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB     # PG13+: stop the slot from filling the disk (slot invalidated instead)
# MySQL: binlog_format=ROW, binlog_row_image=FULL, server_id=..., gtid_mode=ON

Decision gravity. Read from a replica where the engine allows it (MySQL binlog on a replica is common; Postgres logical slots on standbys arrived in PG16). It protects the primary but adds replica lag and an extra failure point. Reversible, but changing the position source requires care to avoid gaps (use GTIDs). Set max_slot_wal_keep_size so a dead consumer sacrifices CDC, not the primary.

Industry examples. Debezium + Kafka at many companies; Shopify and Zendesk have written about it; Netflix DBLog; Stripe and others mention CDC feeding data warehouses.

Everyday analogy. A news agency (connector) copies every dispatch (change) from a clerk's logbook and teletypes it to many newspapers (consumers).

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving a replication slot orphaned after decommissioning a consumer.
  • Using a statement-based binlog (non-deterministic and unusable by CDC).
  • One giant topic for all tables with no keying.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
How log-based capture works

Every ACID database first writes changes to a sequential log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog/redo, MongoDB oplog) before applying them to data files, so it can recover after a crash and feed replicas. CDC is "a replica that outputs events instead of storing tables".

  • Postgres: wal_level=logical, create a publication (which tables) and a replication slot (a server-side bookmark that guarantees WAL is not deleted until confirmed). The connector streams decoded changes in commit order and sends back confirmed_flush_lsn.
  • MySQL: the connector registers as a replica (needs REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT), reads binlog events and tracks file+position or GTID.

Events are emitted at commit, in commit order, with the transaction id, so a consumer can reassemble a transaction. Large transactions (millions of rows) are streamed in chunks in newer versions; confirm behaviour for your version.

Why not the alternatives

Approach Sees deletes Order Load on source Gotcha
Polling updated_at No Weak Heavy queries Misses rows committed late, clock skew
Triggers writing an audit table Yes Yes Adds latency to every write Slows OLTP, schema drift
Dual write (app writes DB and Kafka) Maybe No None Inconsistent when one write fails
Log-based CDC Yes Yes Very low Needs DB config and log access

Decision gravity. Log-based CDC makes the database log (previously an internal detail) a public integration point. The source team must treat log retention and schema as a contract. Hard to retreat from, but the biggest operational win in data integration.

Everyday analogy. A bank keeps a journal of every transaction for audits; CDC just reads that journal.

Common interview traps.

  • Using triggers "because they are easy" and then hitting write latency.
  • Forgetting the replication slot keeps WAL on disk.
  • Believing CDC captures reads.

Initial snapshot without downtime

Problem: the table already holds 500 GB. A consumer needs the full state, then the changes after it, with no gap and no long lock.

Debezium approach: record the current log position (LSN), take a consistent snapshot read (a transaction at repeatable-read isolation), emit rows as op=r, then switch to streaming from the recorded LSN. Short global read lock (MySQL) or none (Postgres exported snapshot).

Netflix DBLog approach: incremental snapshots interleaved with the live stream. Take chunks by primary key range (SELECT ... WHERE id > last ORDER BY id LIMIT 10000), write watermarks to a table before and after each chunk, and drop chunk rows that were also modified in the log between the watermarks. This lets you re-snapshot a single table anytime, pause and resume, without stopping log streaming.

-- Chunk read of the incremental snapshot (PK order, resumable)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 10000;

Decision gravity. Prefer incremental snapshots from day one; the initial blocking snapshot is easy but you will need to re-snapshot (new consumer, bug fix, new table), so the ability to repeat it online is worth the complexity. Reversible.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: new search index has rows that were deleted in the source. Cause: snapshot rows applied after a delete event for the same key arrived. Fix: apply events with a version/LSN comparison (last-write-wins by LSN), and honour tombstones.

Everyday analogy. Photocopying a ledger while clerks keep writing in it; you note the page number at the start so you can add the later entries after.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying the table first, then starting the stream (changes in between are lost).
  • Locking the production table for the snapshot.
  • Not handling deletes that race with snapshot rows.

Ordering, partitioning and delivery guarantees

Key each event by primary key so all changes to a row land in the same Kafka partition and arrive in order. Different rows have no relative order across partitions; for cross-row transaction order, include transaction.id and use the transaction metadata topic, or give the group a single partition per aggregate.

  • Delivery is at-least-once: a connector crash after publishing and before committing its offset replays some events. Consumers must be idempotent: upsert by primary key, ignore events with lower LSN than stored.
  • Kafka Connect exactly-once source support exists in recent versions (KIP-618), but sinks still need idempotent writes; design for duplicates regardless.
  • Tombstones: a delete produces the delete event and a null-value record (for log compaction). Compacted topics (cleanup.policy=compact) can then act as the latest-state table per key and serve as a bootstrap source for new consumers without hitting the database.
-- Idempotent sink upsert guarded by a version
INSERT INTO orders_search (id, status, lsn) VALUES ($1,$2,$3)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET status=EXCLUDED.status, lsn=EXCLUDED.lsn
WHERE orders_search.lsn < EXCLUDED.lsn;

Decision gravity. Partition count and key choice are one-way doors (changing breaks ordering history). Choose the primary key (or aggregate id) as key and size partitions for the future (for example 12 to 48 per busy table).

Everyday analogy. Putting each customer's mail in their own pigeonhole so letters in a pigeonhole stay in the order they came.

Common interview traps.

  • Random partitioning (delete arrives before insert on a consumer).
  • Non-idempotent sinks (duplicate rows or double counted metrics).
  • Assuming total order across tables.

Schema evolution

Add column: new events carry the extra field; old consumers ignore it if the schema is backward compatible. Drop or rename column: breaking. Process:

  1. Register Avro/Protobuf schemas in a registry with compatibility mode (BACKWARD or FULL).
  2. Expand/contract migrations: add new column, dual populate, migrate consumers, drop old after all consumers moved.
  3. Debezium emits the schema change in a separate schema-history topic (needed to decode older log entries, since the log has no column names in some engines such as MySQL binlog).

Never reuse a column name with a new meaning.

Decision gravity. The event schema is an API with unknown clients; treat breaking changes as a versioned new topic (orders.v2) rather than editing in place. Slower, but reversible and safe.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: warehouse loader crashes on a deploy. Metric: DLQ rate and connector task state FAILED. Cause: column type changed from int to string. Fix: compatible change policy enforced in CI against the registry.

Everyday analogy. Changing the form template: older readers must still understand the new forms.

Common interview traps.

  • Renaming a column in place.
  • No registry, JSON with silent field drift.
  • Forgetting the schema history topic.

Outbox pattern: CDC for microservices

Services need to update their DB and publish an event atomically. Dual write fails. Solution: write the business row and an outbox row in the same transaction; CDC reads the outbox table and publishes to Kafka (Debezium has an outbox event router). The event is guaranteed exactly when the transaction commits.

BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=9001;
INSERT INTO outbox(id, aggregate_id, type, payload)
  VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), '9001', 'OrderPaid', '{"orderId":9001}');
COMMIT;

The outbox table grows; delete rows after publishing (CDC reads the log, so deleting the row right away is fine) or partition by day.

Decision gravity. Outbox beats dual writes and distributed transactions for microservice events; the cost is one more table and an extra moving part (CDC). A one-way architectural commitment: all your integrations then depend on CDC health.

Everyday analogy. Writing the outgoing letter and the "to send" slip in one stroke so the postman can never miss it.

Common interview traps.

  • Publishing to Kafka inside the DB transaction callback (not atomic).
  • Using CDC on the business tables and exposing internal shape instead of a clean outbox event.

Operations: lag, failure and cutover

Metrics to watch:

  • Connector lag (source LSN minus confirmed LSN) and MilliSecondsBehindSource.
  • Replication slot retained WAL (pg_replication_slots, restart_lsn vs current).
  • Kafka consumer lag per group.
  • DLQ count and connector state.
-- Postgres: how much WAL is a slot holding back?
SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Failure cases: connector restarts (resume from last offset, duplicates possible); failover of the source (the new primary must have the slot or a GTID continuation; Postgres logical slots are not carried to a promoted standby before PG17, a classic pain, so plan re-snapshot or slot-sync; confirm the version feature); binlog purged before the connector returns (snapshot again).

Cutover to a new pipeline: run old and new in parallel, compare row counts and checksums on a sample, then switch consumers.

Decision gravity. Alert thresholds on retained WAL (for example 10 GB) are cheap insurance against taking down the primary. Reversible and mandatory.

Everyday analogy. Watching how thick the pile of unread logbook pages is getting.

Common interview traps.

  • No alert on slot retention.
  • Assuming failover keeps CDC position automatically.
  • Reprocessing without idempotent consumers.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Why log-based over polling, triggers and dual writes, with their failure modes.
  • Snapshot plus stream consistency and the watermark idea.
  • Ordering by key, at-least-once plus idempotent consumers, tombstones and compaction.
  • Schema evolution with a registry and expand/contract.
  • Source protection: replication slot WAL retention, reading from replicas, limits.
  • Outbox pattern as the microservice answer.
  • Seniors quantify lag, discuss failover of the source, multi-region, GDPR deletes in an immutable log.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing Kafka but not the source-side internals.
  • Claiming exactly-once end to end without idempotent sinks.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• CDC reads the database's own commit log and publishes ordered row-change events; the better alternative to polling, triggers and dual writes.
  • Setup: Debezium connector, Kafka keyed by primary key, schema registry, sinks (search, cache, warehouse).
  • Snapshot then stream without a gap using a recorded log position or incremental watermark chunks.
  • Delivery is at-least-once; make consumers idempotent with versions (LSN) and handle tombstones.
  • Evolve schemas with compatible changes and versioned topics; the event is a public contract.
  • Guard the source: monitor retained WAL, cap slot size, plan for failover; use the outbox pattern for service events.
